scoreRule: 1 point per correct MC item; 10 points maximum; local provisional grade only
description: Independent environmental reading assessment draft with ten newly authored questions and evidence references; content sign-off pending

questions.q: Why would a sign beside the stream alone have been insufficient?
choices: The stream had no visitors.
Much of the litter arrived through drains from another place.
All rubbish was already collected by volunteers.
The signs were impossible to read.
questions.explanation: The engineer shows that wrappers can move from the bus stop through drainage pipes.

questions.q: Where can rainwater carry rubbish dropped near the bus stop?
choices: Into the library building.
Only into nearby rubbish bins.
Directly into the school playground.
Through drains and pipes towards the stream.
questions.explanation: Rain can move light litter from the street into a drain connected to the stream.

questions.q: Why did the students make their counts when lessons ended?
choices: They wanted to avoid speaking to the driver.
The stream was easiest to see then.
The bus stop was especially busy at that time.
The council had asked them to leave early.
questions.explanation: The students counted after the last lesson because the bus stop was most crowded.

questions.q: What can be inferred from the much higher litter count near the bus stop?
choices: The bus stop was an important source worth investigating.
The library had no visitors at all.
Every wrapper came from the same person.
The stream had already been completely cleaned.
questions.explanation: The large contrast in counts suggests the busy stop was a key location to examine.

questions.q: Why did changing the bin's collection time make sense?
choices: It meant the café could stop serving snacks.
It ensured that drains never needed cleaning.
The bin tended to be full before the afternoon rush.
The students no longer needed to count rubbish.
questions.explanation: The driver explained that a morning collection left the bin full by four o'clock.

questions.q: Why is asking where rubbish begins its journey a useful question?
choices: It encourages action at the source of the problem.
It proves the river itself creates the litter.
It means volunteers should ignore the street.
It removes the need for future observations.
questions.explanation: The final question directs attention to where discarded items enter the drainage route.

questions.q: How did speaking to a café owner help the investigation?
choices: It confirmed that no one bought food near the bus stop.
It linked snack purchases to the busy waiting area.
It showed that the stream was naturally dirty.
It proved the council was entirely responsible.
questions.explanation: The café owner explained that customers bought snacks while waiting for buses.

questions.q: Why could the next storm still reveal a problem?
choices: The stream was far away from the street.
The café had already closed.
Every rubbish bin had been removed.
Wind could bring litter from other streets.
questions.explanation: The students recognise that litter may arrive from further away in different weather.

questions.q: What was gained by inviting neighbours to upload observations?
choices: The council could stop working on drains.
Everyone was forced to clean the stream.
The group could collect evidence from more streets.
The students could identify one person to blame.
questions.explanation: Fifteen residents supplied photographs from nearby roads, broadening the observations.

questions.q: Which lesson follows most directly from the whole project?
choices: Finding causes leads to more targeted action than assigning blame.
Warning signs are the only effective way to prevent litter.
The council should never change a collection schedule.
Rubbish beside the river must always begin there.
questions.explanation: The students move from blaming people at the stream to examining how litter travels there.
